narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 50.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly more likely than passing, but it was enough to place you on the rejection side of the admissions threshold.

The most influential factor was your undergraduate GPA. At 3.40, it was above the accepted-student average of 3.23, so this factor actually pushed your prediction toward passing. However, the next two most important factors worked against you and outweighed that positive signal. Your third-year class standing was the second-strongest influence: your decile of 2 was far from the accepted average of about 5.8, and the model treated this as a meaningful warning sign for bar failure. Your first-year decile of 2 was the third-strongest influence; compared with an accepted average of 6.0, it also pushed the prediction toward failure. In short, your GPA helped, but the two low class-standing indicators drove the final denial.

As next steps, ask admissions for a human review of your file and provide any context that explains your class standing, such as illness, work obligations, or an upward trend. Consider retaking the LSAT with structured preparation, strengthen your academic record if possible, and apply to programs that use holistic review rather than a single predictive cutoff.
